I couldn't find anything for v. 2 apart from what's grouped with v. 1, and nothing on v. 7 by itself, so those verses are combined with their neighbours. The Clarke notes come from his full Jonah 3 page on Bible Hub. I read that page in full, but it isn't set up for quote-level citations, so those points carry only the link.

# Jonah 3: Research notes

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**vv. 1–2: The second call**
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** The second call shows God's love for His wayward people. Jonah had resisted, but once he repented God called him again, though He didn't have to. "He did it out of mercy and grace." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-3/
- **Guzik:** This time God doesn't tell Jonah to "cry out against" Nineveh. He tells him to go and wait for further instructions. Guzik suggests God often leads one step at a time because He only tells us what we can handle.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-3/
- **Matthew Henry:** Giving Jonah his job back showed God had fully forgiven his earlier disobedience. Henry compares it to a pardon.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_003.cfm
- **Matthew Henry:** God didn't soften the message to suit Jonah. He had to preach exactly what he had once refused to preach.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_003.cfm
- **Gill:** The commission had to be renewed, because going ahead on the old one without a fresh word would have been dangerous. Gill compares Israel going up without God's word in Numbers 14. The renewal also shows Jonah was still a prophet despite his failings.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/3-1.htm
- **Geneva Study Bible:** Taking Jonah back is a great display of God's mercy.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/3-1.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The Hebrew word for "message" means a proclamation, the same idea as the Greek *kerygma* in the Septuagint.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/3-1.htm
- **Clarke:** The phrase means "cry the cry that I bid thee." It is the language of a herald, like John the Baptist or the apostles. Clarke says preaching to souls calls for real earnestness, but not "screaming rant." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jonah/3.htm
- **Bible.org:** God's words were almost exactly the same as His first command.  https://bible.org/seriespage/nineveh%E2%80%99s-repentance-and-jonah%E2%80%99s-wrath-jonah-3-4

**v. 3: Jonah obeys; the city's size**
- **Matthew Henry:** Jonah didn't sit still in sloth or sulking. He went straight to a distant city he had probably never seen.  https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_003.cfm
- **Benson:** Jonah now obeyed without reluctance, which was the fruit of God's correction.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/3-1.htm
- **The city's size:** One commentary on Bible Hub says Nineveh was a cluster of cities with open spaces and could well be three days' journey around.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/3-1.htm
- **Clarke:** Citing ancient writers (Strabo, Diodorus), Clarke puts the circumference at 54–60 miles. It would take three days to walk round it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jonah/3.htm

**v. 4: "Forty more days"**
- **Guzik:** This was surely not Jonah's whole sermon, but it was his emphasis: what would happen if they didn't repent.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-3/
- **Barnes:** If God had meant to destroy the city no matter what, He would have done it without warning. The word "yet" points to God's patience.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/jonah-3.html
- **Matthew Henry (as quoted on Bible Hub):** Forty days is a long delay for a just God, but a short time for a guilty people to change. Henry applies it to readiness for death.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/3-1.htm
- **Clarke (text note):** The Septuagint reads "three days," probably a copyist's mistake. The Hebrew "forty" is the true reading. Forty days gave time to think and repent; three days would only have caused terror. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jonah/3.htm
- **Bible.org:** The message was a warning, not just a prediction, and the Ninevites were right to hear it as a call to repent.  https://bible.org/seriespage/nineveh%E2%80%99s-repentance-and-jonah%E2%80%99s-wrath-jonah-3-4

**v. 5: "The Ninevites believed God"**
- **Guzik:** The word "repentance" isn't in the passage, but the people did repent.  Repentance starts with believing God.  Real revival starts with faithful preaching and hearing of God's word.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-3/
- **Matthew Henry:** They took Jonah's words as God's word. Despite their many gods, they believed in one living God to whom they were accountable.  Henry also notes that Jonah preached one sermon with no miracles, and they responded while Israel stayed stubborn.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_003.cfm
- **Bible Hub Study Bible:** This was not just fear of disaster but "faith that bore visible fruit in repentance". It links the verse to Jesus' words in Matthew 12:41.  https://biblehub.com/jonah/3-5.htm
- **Clarke:** They knew the threat was conditional, even though that wasn't stated. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jonah/3.htm
- **MacArthur (background):** Two plagues (765 and 759 BC) and a solar eclipse (763 BC) may have prepared the city for Jonah's message.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/macarthur_john/bible-introductions/jonah-intro.cfm

**v. 6: The king**
- **Matthew Henry:** The king rose from his throne out of reverence for God's word, fear of His wrath, and sorrow for sin.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jon/Jon_003.cfm
- **Clarke:** Clarke lists guesses about the king's identity (Pul, Sardanapalus, or a contemporary of Joash). He notes the fast became general because the king decreed it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jonah/3.htm

**vv. 7–8: The decree; animals in sackcloth; turning from violence**
- **Guzik:** They even dressed their animals as if in mourning.  Repentance means crying out to God with passion.  It means turning from evil and violence, not making excuses.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-3/
- **Expositor's Bible:** In the time of the Old Testament, a national repentance would naturally be organised by the rulers. Animals took part as they did in Eastern funeral customs.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/jonah/3-10.html
- **Clarke:** The animals were included so that everything people saw would deepen the impression. He gives classical parallels from Virgil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jonah/3.htm

**v. 9: "Who knows?"**
- **Guzik:** Repentance hopes in God's mercy.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-3/
- **Clarke:** "There is at least a peradventure" (a chance) of being saved. God takes no pleasure in sinners' death and has Himself told people to repent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jonah/3.htm

**v. 10: God relents**
- **Guzik:** Repentance appeals to God's mercy, not His justice; it doesn't oblige Him.  Jonah was not a false prophet, for two reasons. The warning carried an implied "if you do not repent" (Jeremiah 18). And God did judge Nineveh later, as Nahum records, after holding off for about 150 years.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-3/
- **Barnes:** God didn't really change. The whole point of the threat was that He would not have to carry it out. His threats are conditional, just as His promises are.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/jonah-3.html
- **Commentary on Bible Hub:** It points out the word "turn" used of both people and God in vv. 8–10, and the bold use of "repent" for God, as in Exodus 32:14.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/3-1.htm

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ (mainly v. 10, with a link to v. 5)

Everyone I read agrees God's character doesn't change. They differ on how to describe His "relenting," and on what part the Ninevites' works played.

- **Reformed (Calvin):** The Ninevites were pardoned through repentance. God looked at their real change of life, not just outward rituals.  But Jonah is reporting what happened, not giving the cause. Other Scriptures teach whether pardon is free or earned.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/jonah/3-10.html
- **Reformed Baptist (Gill):** God didn't repent of His decrees, only of the threat. What changed was "not of his mind and will concerning them, but of his outward dispensations towards them" (how He dealt with them). https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/jonah/3-10.html
- **Baptist (MacArthur, GTY):** God may respond differently to different human responses.  On whether God changed: "No, it was Nineveh that changed". https://www.gty.org/library/blog/B170209/our-unchanging-god
- **Charismatic (Sam Storms):** God's unchanging nature actually *required* Him to treat Nineveh differently once it repented.  His stated purpose is to punish the wicked "unless they repent."  https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/did-god-change-his-mind-about-judging-the-ninevites
  - Storms also says events like this are "the execution in time of purposes eternally existing in the mind of God". https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/the-immutability-of-god/
- **Lutheran (LCMS):** This one is warmer to real divine response. Prayer is meant to make God act, not just to change us.  God changes His mind and heart without undermining His unchanging nature, and the article cites v. 9.  https://witness.lcms.org/2024/do-our-prayers-change-anything/
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** Clarke says God "changed his purpose." He frames the purpose itself as conditional: destroy the city if they don't turn within forty days. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/jonah/3.htm
- **Open theism vs. the traditional view (Don Stewart):** Open theists see this as God's mind actually changing.  The traditional view is that God knew all along they would repent.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/does-god-know-everything/27-did-god-change-his-mind-about-nineveh.cfm
- **GotQuestions:** "God did not change His mind; rather, His message to Nineveh was a warning meant to provoke repentance". https://www.gotquestions.org/God-change-mind.html

## 3. Other views

**Catholic**
- **Catholic Encyclopedia:** Its summary says the authorities ordered repentance and God spared the city.  It also discusses arguments about whether the book is historical. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08497b.htm
- **Clement of Rome:** The Ninevites "propitiated God by prayer, and obtained salvation, although they were aliens" to God's covenant. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1010.htm
- **Justin Martyr:** He describes the fast of men and beasts as true repentance, done in the belief that God is merciful.  https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/anf01.viii.iv.cvii.html
- **Augustine (summarised by Bible.org):** He used the fasting Ninevite children as part of his argument for original sin.  https://bible.org/seriespage/chapter-3-fasting-through-patristic-era

**Orthodox (OCA)**
- **Fr. John Breck:** Following St Cyril of Jerusalem, he says Jonah and Jesus were both sent to preach repentance.  In Luke's Gospel the "sign of Jonah" is Jonah's *preaching* to Nineveh.  https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/the-sign-of-jonah
- **OCA life of the prophet:** Links Nineveh's repentance to Matthew 12:41.  https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2014/09/22/102696-prophet-jonah

**Modern scholarship**
- **Bible Odyssey:** Scholars see humour in the king's dramatic decree and especially in the animals fasting and wearing mourning clothes (v. 8). Some class the book as satire or parody, readings that only became standard in modern times.  https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/humor-in-the-book-of-jonah/
- **Constable:** Since the 19th century, many have read the book as allegory or parable rather than history.  He quotes Leslie Allen: the book shows how and why a prophecy was *not* fulfilled.  Constable himself calls it historical narrative.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jonah.html
- **TGC course:** Even this evangelical source calls the book satire and points to its humour and exaggeration.  https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/course/jonah/

**What I didn't find:** NET Bible notes, the Pulpit Commentary or Ellicott, Precept Austin's verse notes on Jonah 3, Anglican teachers, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. The search allowance ran out, so I couldn't look further.
